The must-sees

  • Basilica of Sant’Ambrogio

    Church

    Saint Ambrose, the city’s patron and bishop, founded the church in the late 4th century and is buried in its crypt. The present building is largely Romanesque, from the 11th and 12th centuries.

    Look for: In the square beside the church, an old Roman column has two holes said to be left by the devil’s horns after he charged at Ambrose.

  • Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II

    Shopping · 1877

    Giuseppe Mengoni designed it and died in a fall from the scaffolding shortly before it was finished in 1877. Visitors spin on their heel over the mosaic bull in the floor for luck.

    Look for: Under the central glass dome, the floor mosaics show the arms of Milan, Turin, Florence and Rome. The bull is Turin’s.

  • La Scala

    Culture · 1778

    Giuseppe Piermarini designed the theatre, which opened in 1778 on the site of the church of Santa Maria alla Scala. Many of Verdi’s and Puccini’s operas had their premieres here.

    Look for: In the small square in front, Leonardo da Vinci stands on a tall pedestal, ringed by four of his pupils.

  • Milan Cathedral

    Church

    Work began in 1386 and went on for centuries; the façade was only finished in the early 1800s under Napoleon. The gilded Madonnina on the highest spire has watched over the city since 1774.

    Look for: Inside, high in the vault above the altar, a small red light marks where a nail said to be from the Cross is kept.

  • Navigli

    Waterfront

    Milan was once linked to lakes and rivers by a network of navigable canals, and marble for the Duomo arrived by boat. Most canals were covered over in the 1930s; the Naviglio Grande and Naviglio Pavese remain.

    Look for: Along the Naviglio Grande, find the Vicolo dei Lavandai, an alley where stone washboards still line a small canal.

  • Piazza del Duomo

    Square

    The square took its present shape in the late 19th century, when old blocks were cleared around the cathedral. An equestrian statue of King Victor Emmanuel II stands in the middle.

    Look for: On the south side stand the two pale Arengario buildings, begun in the 1930s. The one beside Palazzo Reale holds the Museo del Novecento, Milan’s museum of 20th-century art.

  • Pinacoteca di Brera

    Museum · 1809

    The gallery opened in 1809 to show works gathered from churches and convents under Napoleon. It holds Mantegna’s Lamentation over the Dead Christ and Raphael’s Marriage of the Virgin.

    Look for: The bronze Napoleon in the courtyard is nude, a cast of Canova’s statue showing him as Mars the Peacemaker.

  • Santa Maria delle Grazie and The Last Supper

    Church

    Leonardo painted the Last Supper on the refectory wall in the 1490s for Ludovico Sforza. When bombs destroyed much of the refectory in 1943, the wall with the painting survived behind sandbags.

    Look for: On the opposite wall, Montorfano’s Crucifixion, a true fresco from 1495, has kept its colour far better.

  • Sforza Castle

    Fortress

    Francesco Sforza rebuilt an older Visconti fortress here in the 15th century, and Leonardo worked for the court. Among its museums is Michelangelo’s last, unfinished sculpture, the Rondanini Pietà.

    Look for: In the Sala delle Asse, Leonardo painted the ceiling as a pergola of interlaced trees, their branches knotted with a golden rope.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in Milan and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your Milan passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
